hazards.name: Hoh side-channel fords before Olympus Guard Station
hazards.season: Any time after moderate to heavy rain; highest October-June and during warm-weather snowmelt
hazards.real_world: Two stream crossings near mile 8 must be forded. In dry spells they are nearly dry; in moderate to heavy rain they can become impassable (NPS 2026).
hazards.game_event_idea: The braid runs brown and loud after a night of rain. Options: (A) Wade now: unbuckle hip belt, face upstream, use poles - success 85% with trekking poles, 60% without; failure = soaked gear and a dropped item. (B) Wait for the river to drop: lose half a day; 70% chance it is ankle-deep by morning; costs one extra food day. (C) Scout upstream for a log: 50% find one; slip chance 20% without good boots. (D) Turn back to Happy Four and enjoy a shorter trip.

hazards.name: Glacier Meadows washout ladder
hazards.season: Year-round; worst with snow, ice or rain; rockfall any time
hazards.real_world: About a quarter mile before Glacier Meadows, a ~100-ft cable/rope ladder crosses a loose avalanche-chute washout. In 2026 it had several broken, cracked or missing rungs, was anchored to a dead tree with exposed roots, and had rockfall risk and midday queues. Guidebooks suggest camping below it with heavy packs.
hazards.game_event_idea: The ladder sways over the gully; a pebble clicks down past you. Options: (A) Climb with your full pack - success depends on pack weight: under 30 lb 95%, 30-45 lb 85%, over 45 lb 70%; failure = scraped hands, dropped trekking pole or twisted ankle. (B) Lower your pack on a cord first (requires 30 ft of cord/rope) - 98%. (C) Wear a helmet - rockfall injury chance drops from 10% to 2%. (D) Camp at Elk Lake and day-hike past it tomorrow with a light pack.

hazards.name: Steep snow in the avalanche chutes above Elk Lake
hazards.season: Winter through early summer (often into July); winter travel above Elk Lake not recommended
hazards.real_world: Steep snow slopes cross avalanche chutes between Elk Lake and Glacier Meadows; an ice axe may be required, the trail can be hidden, and in winter ropes and anchors may be needed (NPS).
hazards.game_event_idea: A hard, icy snow tongue fills the chute; the runout ends in rocks. Options: (A) Kick steps with ice axe - 95% (axe + self-arrest skill), 75% axe only. (B) Wait for the sun to soften it (lose 2 hours) - +10% success. (C) Cross without an axe - 55%; a slip without an axe ends the trip with a rescue in gentle mode. (D) Turn around and camp at Elk Lake.

hazards.name: Knife-edge lateral moraine and scree descent to the Blue Glacier
hazards.season: Climbing season (late June-mid August); conditions worsen as the glacier thins
hazards.real_world: The moraine crest is a narrow ridge with steep drops; climbers must stay high until a double cairn/white pole marks a faint, loose descent of about 400 vertical ft to the ice. Climbers call it the crux and report it getting worse.
hazards.game_event_idea: Fog rolls in on the moraine crest. Options: (A) Follow the cairns slowly - navigation check: 90% with GPS track, 70% with map and compass, 50% neither. (B) Drop down early where it looks easier - 40% cliffed out, lose 2 hours. (C) Wait for the fog to lift (lose 1 hour, 60% it lifts). (D) Call it a viewpoint day and enjoy the glacier from above.

hazards.name: Crevasses on the Blue Glacier
hazards.season: Late June-mid August climbing season; snow bridges weaken through the day and season
hazards.real_world: Glacier travel with crevasses from finger-width to a couple of feet on the lower glacier and larger ones higher up; NPS says only experienced mountaineers with glacier travel and crevasse rescue skills and gear should attempt Mount Olympus.
hazards.game_event_idea: A sagging line in the snow crosses your path. Options: (A) Rope up and probe - crevasse-fall chance 2%, and a fall is held. (B) Walk unroped - fall chance 10%; in gentle mode a fall means a helicopter rescue and the trip ends; in Sierra mode it is fatal. (C) Detour wide around the sag (lose 30 min, chance 1%). Percentages double after 1 pm (soft bridges).

hazards.name: Snow Dome steep runout traverse and afternoon blue ice
hazards.real_world: Reported as the route's biggest objective hazard: a steep runout snow traverse in the morning and a ~200-ft descending traverse on slushy blue ice in the afternoon; pickets and ice screws advised.
hazards.game_event_idea: Hard morning snow tilts toward a drop. Options: (A) Place pickets as running protection (slow, 98%). (B) Move together without protection (fast, 85%). (C) Wait until the snow softens (lose 1 hour; afternoon blue ice later is worse).

hazards.name: Bergschrund and snow wall at Crystal Pass
hazards.real_world: Late season, a wide bergschrund can span the glacier below Crystal Pass; one report found an open crevasse splitting the bootpath and a ~30-ft, ~60-degree snow wall.
hazards.game_event_idea: The bootpath ends at a blue-black gap. Options: (A) Cross the remaining snow bridge roped (80%). (B) Climb the steep snow wall with two tools (needs a second tool or good axe skill; 85%). (C) Try the direct 'Fourth of July' line instead (great in June, mostly impassable after late June). (D) Turn around - the Snow Dome view is your summit.

hazards.name: Fifth-class summit block and rappel
hazards.real_world: One short pitch of low-to-mid fifth-class rock (about 5.4) on the North Ridge with a rappel off; the steep snow gully off the false summit is a rockfall/sliding 'bowling alley'.
hazards.game_event_idea: The final tower is wet and a cloud is building. Options: (A) Lead the pitch (needs rock rack and rope; 90% dry, 70% wet). (B) Scramble the loose east side (class 4, 75%, rockfall 10%). (C) Set a turnaround time and stop at the false summit - a gentle 'almost' ending with full sketch credit.

hazards.name: Storms and whiteouts on Mount Olympus
hazards.season: Any season; storms move in quickly off the Pacific
hazards.real_world: The summit area is one of the wettest places in the contiguous US; climbers report finding the route hard without a boot path, and storms move quickly (NPS).
hazards.game_event_idea: Morning: grey cap on the summit, wind rising. Options: (A) Go anyway (summit chance 40%, lost-route chance 25%). (B) Wait a day at camp (costs one food day; 60% clear tomorrow). (C) Descend now (safe; trip ends without summit).

hazards.name: Queets River ford
hazards.season: Usually feasible only late July-September; generally not fordable late fall, winter or spring
hazards.real_world: Required ford at the trailhead, commonly waist deep in summer; NPS suggests flow at the Hwy 101 gauge under 800 cfs, and flow can rise within hours. It can be impassable on the way out even if fine on the way in.
hazards.game_event_idea: On the way out, the river is higher than when you came in. Options: (A) Cross now with poles and a partner (success scales with flow: low 90%, moderate 60%, high 25%; failure in gentle mode = swept, gear lost, rescue; Sierra mode = drowning). (B) Wait a day on the far bank (needs an extra food day; 70% chance it drops). (C) Link arms in a group of three (+15%). (D) Never start if rain is forecast (planning screen choice).

hazards.name: Upper Bogachiel washouts, brush and faint trail
hazards.real_world: Washouts near Mosquito Creek (steep detour, short exposed section) and between Flapjack and 15 Mile; above 15 Mile the trail is difficult to follow; dense brush to the Mink Lake junction.
hazards.game_event_idea: The tread vanishes into salmonberry taller than your head. Options: (A) Bushwhack along the river (slow; 20% chance to soak and lose a dry layer). (B) Backtrack to the last sure tread and search (lose 1 hour, 80% find it). (C) Use map, compass or GPS (95%). (D) Camp early at 15 Mile and decide tomorrow.

hazards.name: Bogachiel and Calawah fords on the Snider-Jackson trails
hazards.season: Any time after rain; easiest late summer
hazards.real_world: NPS: the Bogachiel must be forded on the South Snider-Jackson route and often runs deep; the Calawah ford on the North Snider-Jackson can become hazardous at any time.
hazards.game_event_idea: Same ford mechanic as the Queets with smaller rivers: (A) Wade (low flow 95%, after rain 60%). (B) Wait. (C) Retreat over the ridge (long, dry, 10 miles without water).

hazards.name: Hot, dry climb through the 1978 burn
hazards.real_world: Steep, exposed grade with 22 switchbacks and little canopy through the 1978 Hoh Fire burn; no water until C.B. Flats (NPS 2026).
hazards.game_event_idea: Halfway up, the sun bakes the silver snags. Options: (A) Push on (if water carried under 2 L: 30% heat exhaustion - lose half a day). (B) Rest in the only shade (lose 1 hour). (C) Planning choice: start at dawn and carry 3 L (no risk).

hazards.name: Black bears and food storage
hazards.real_world: Approved bear canisters are required for all overnight wilderness stays (2026); bear wires and hangs are not acceptable; elk and bear are frequently seen on the Hoh Lake Trail in summer and fall.
hazards.game_event_idea: A bear noses around camp at dusk. Outcome depends on packing: canister locked and 100 ft from tent = bear wanders off (98%). Canister unlocked = 40% bear gets food, trip ends early and a ranger write-up. No canister (hang or tent) = 70% food lost, trip ends; also a citation event at the trailhead check.

hazards.name: Rutting bull elk
hazards.real_world: Bulls bugle, spar and chase; Hoh-area elk are habituated, and the park has closed the Hoh campground for the rut. Keep at least 50 yards (park release) and back away from aggressive animals.
hazards.game_event_idea: A bull steps onto the trail, grinding his teeth. Options: (A) Back away slowly and detour through the trees (lose 20 min, safe). (B) Wait behind a big tree (safe, lose 40 min). (C) Try to pass close for a photo (30% charged - trampled pack, minor injury).

hazards.name: Rain forest rain and cold
hazards.real_world: The Hoh Rain Forest averages about 140 inches of precipitation a year (NPS); higher camps can be cold and wet even in summer.
hazards.game_event_idea: Third day of steady rain. Outcome by packing: rain jacket + synthetic/wool layers + dry bag = morale fine. Cotton or no pack liner = 40% chance 'wet and shivering' status (must turn back or rest a day). Options: (A) Hole up in the Happy Four shelter. (B) Hike fast to stay warm. (C) Turn back.

hazards.name: Blowdown and storm damage
hazards.season: Winter and spring storms; crews clear in summer
hazards.real_world: In June 2026 NPS counted 37 downed trees between the Hoh trailhead and Glacier Meadows; in July 2026, 29 between the Queets ford and Bob Creek.
hazards.game_event_idea: A giant spruce lies across the trail chest-high. Options: (A) Climb over (10% slip, scraped shin). (B) Crawl under (pack snags; 5% tears a strap). (C) Detour through the root wad mud (lose 15 min).

hazards.name: Trying the Blue Glacier as a day hike
hazards.real_world: The lateral moraine is 18.5 miles one way (37 miles round trip, ~5,100 ft gain); there is no camping between Glacier Meadows and the Blue Glacier and the upper camps are quota-limited.
hazards.game_event_idea: The player chose 'day hike' gear for the Blue Glacier. At mile 13 (High Hoh Bridge) at 3 pm: (A) Push on - darkness on the ladder, 50% forced bivy without a sleeping bag (cold, hungry, ranger finds you in the morning in gentle mode). (B) Turn back now (arrive at the car after dark; fine with a headlamp, 30% fall without one). (C) Beg a spare spot at a camp - not allowed without a permit; ranger event.

hazards.name: Quota camps full (Martin Creek, Elk Lake, Glacier Meadows, Hoh Lake, C.B. Flats)
hazards.real_world: These are quota areas; permits are limited and changes must be made before the trip. Camping is allowed only at the camp on your permit.
hazards.game_event_idea: Planning screen: Glacier Meadows shows FULL for your dates. Options: (A) Shift dates midweek (70% open). (B) Camp at Lewis Meadow or the 13-mile sites and do a long day to the moraine. (C) Book Elk Lake instead and day-hike over the ladder. (D) Go after October 15 when quotas end - but snow and short days arrive.

hazards.name: Road delays: US 101 Hoh River Bridge closures and Hoh entrance lines
hazards.season: Bridge: September-October 2026 closures, one-lane signals ongoing; entrance lines: summer
hazards.real_world: WSDOT closed the US 101 Hoh River Bridge (MP 176.5) for up to six days at a time in fall 2026 with a ~4-hour detour; summer waits at the Hoh entrance station reach two hours.
hazards.game_event_idea: Drive-to-trailhead scene: (A) Leave at 5 am - no line, sunrise elk. (B) Leave at 10 am - 50% two-hour wait, start hiking at 1 pm (shorter first day). (C) Trailhead south of a closed bridge - 4-hour detour or pick a different trailhead.

hazards.name: Standing dead trees in the Paradise Fire burn
hazards.real_world: The 2015 Paradise Fire burned the upper Queets; NPS says camping past Bob Creek is not recommended due to standing dead trees and the trail is hard to follow.
hazards.game_event_idea: Wind rises at a burned camp. Options: (A) Pitch under the snags (10% a limb falls near you - scare in gentle mode). (B) Walk back to Bob Creek in the dusk (safe, tiring). (C) Camp on an open gravel bar (safe if river low).

hazards.name: Untreated water
hazards.real_world: NPS: boil, filter or chemically treat all water to prevent Giardia; glacial water is silty.
hazards.game_event_idea: Your filter clogs on silty Hoh water. Options: (A) Let a pot settle overnight then filter (slow, safe). (B) Use backup tablets (safe if packed). (C) Drink untreated (10% stomach trouble a week later - comic epilogue).

hazards.name: Early autumn snow and short days
hazards.real_world: After the quota season ends October 15, upper Hoh camps are open but early snow, avalanche chutes and short daylight make the upper trail much harder; NPS does not recommend winter travel above Elk Lake.
hazards.game_event_idea: Morning at Elk Lake: four inches of new snow. Options: (A) Continue to Glacier Meadows (needs traction + axe; ladder icy 60%). (B) Enjoy a snowy layover at Elk Lake. (C) Head down early.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Roosevelt elk
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Large herds graze the river meadows; bulls bugle and spar in the September-October rut. Keep at least 50 yards away (park release; the elk page asks for 100 ft).
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Helper/advisor character (an old cow elk who knows the river crossings) and a rut hazard; sketchable.

wildlife_and_plants.name: American black bear
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Frequently seen on the Hoh Lake Trail in summer and early fall (NPS); bears seen near the South Fork Hoh DNR campground.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Homage nod to the book's Bear: a calm bear met at a berry patch who teaches 'keep your food locked'; sketchable.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Cougar (mountain lion)
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Present park-wide but rarely seen; tracks on gravel bars are more likely than sightings.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Tracks-in-the-mud journal entry; rare tense encounter (stand tall, do not run).

wildlife_and_plants.name: Banana slug
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Bright yellow slugs on the rain forest floor and trail after rain.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Comic sketch target; slows you down if you stop to count them.

wildlife_and_plants.name: American dipper
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Small grey bird that bobs on rocks and walks underwater in fast streams.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Guide bird that shows the safest place to cross a stream (bonus to ford chance if you watched it).

wildlife_and_plants.name: Pacific wren
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Tiny brown bird with an enormous bubbling song in old-growth understory.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Morning song cue; sketchable.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Varied thrush
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Its single long, eerie whistle carries through foggy forest.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Sound-only creature in fog scenes; journal riddle.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Bald eagle
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Hunts salmon along the big rivers.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Sky sprite over river scenes; sketchable.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Salmon and steelhead (coho, winter steelhead)
wildlife_and_plants.notes: The Hoh and Queets are wild salmon rivers; an interpretive sign at the Hoh notes coho in Taft Creek. No fishing license needed in the park, but regulations apply.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Optional fishing mini-choice (needs tackle; affects food).

wildlife_and_plants.name: Douglas squirrel
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Chattering little red squirrel that scolds hikers from conifer branches.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Scolding alarm event if food is left out.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Rough-skinned newt
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Slow orange-bellied newt of ponds and wet trails; toxic skin - do not handle.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Sketch, don't touch lesson.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Olympic marmot
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Endemic marmot of subalpine meadows; more common on the High Divide side of Hoh Lake. Presence at specific Hoh-region sites unverified.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Whistling lookout helper near the top of the Hoh Lake Trail; sketchable endemic.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Sitka spruce
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Signature giant of the west-side valleys, often growing in rows (colonnades) on old nurse logs.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Field-guide spread entry; scale reference in scenes.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Western hemlock and nurse logs
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Hemlock seedlings sprout on fallen logs, leaving stilted roots when the log rots away.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Sketchable 'tree on stilts' journal entry.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Western redcedar
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Fluted red trunks and stringy bark at the Cedar Grove (4.0 mi).
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Field-guide entry; shelter-from-rain choice under a big cedar.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Bigleaf maple with club moss (Selaginella oregana)
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Maples draped in club moss give the Hall of Mosses its name (NPS).
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Signature opening-scene sketch.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Douglas-fir (Queets Fir)
wildlife_and_plants.notes: The abandoned spur near Coal Creek leads toward a Douglas-fir once famed as among the largest in the world; the path is nearly impossible to follow.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Optional risky detour for a rare journal page.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Licorice fern and sword fern
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Licorice fern grows from mossy branches; sword fern carpets the floor.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Field-guide entries.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Devil's club
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Huge maple-like leaves on spiny stems; painful to grab while bushwhacking.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Brush hazard; gloves mitigate.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Stinging nettle
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Brushy, thorny open fields on the Queets include nettles (WTA).
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Shorts-vs-pants packing consequence.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Salmonberry, thimbleberry and huckleberries
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Berries along brushy trails in summer; huckleberries near the Mink Lake junction in late summer (2023 report).
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Snack bonus; also attracts bears (shared berry patch scene).

wildlife_and_plants.name: Skunk cabbage
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Bright yellow spathes in spring swamps; skunky smell.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Spring-only sketch.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Lettuce lichen / lungwort (Lobaria) and beard lichens
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Leafy green lichens fall from old-growth canopies after storms; pale beard lichens hang from branches.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Field-guide entries; 'gift from the canopy' after wind.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Chanterelles and other autumn mushrooms
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Autumn fungi on the rain forest floor. Check park gathering rules before picking anything; the game should model sketching rather than picking.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Sketch-not-pick choice, echoing the homage's ending.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Subalpine fir, mountain hemlock and heather
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Spire-shaped firs and pink heather at Glacier Meadows' subalpine parkland.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Scene palette transition from rain forest to alpine.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Avalanche lily and glacier lily
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Early-summer lilies blooming right at the edge of melting snow (general subalpine Olympic flora; exact sites unverified).
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Seasonal sketch that only appears in July.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Olympic Mountain groundsel (Senecio neowebsteri)
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Rare yellow composite endemic to the Olympic Mountains, growing on alpine talus; flowers late summer (mid-July to mid-September observations). Occurrence on the Mount Olympus massif specifically is unverified.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Candidate real-world 'golden glow' analog: a small golden flower on high scree, found only after camping high and watching the sunset - to be sketched, never picked.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Piper's bellflower (Campanula piperi)
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Olympic endemic of high rock crevices with blue star-shaped flowers (site-specific occurrence unverified).
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Rare endemic sketch for the journal.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Snow algae (watermelon snow)
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Pinkish algae tint summer snowfields; do not eat the snow.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Mysterious pink snow sketch; a gentle science note.

permit_and_rules.rule: A wilderness permit is required for every overnight stay in the park wilderness, year-round, by advance reservation on Recreation.gov; the WIC issues it 3 days before the trip and you print it yourself.

Fees: $6 non-refundable reservation fee per permit plus $8 per adult (16+) per night; youth 15 and under free; Annual Wilderness Pass $45 covers nightly fees for the holder. Permit holder must be at least 16.

2026 reservation windows: summer season (May 15-October 15) opened April 15, 2026 at 7 am; Glacier Meadows/Elk Lake reservation season June 15-October 15, 2026; winter season (October 16-May 14) reservations opened September 15, 2026.

Quota areas include Hoh Lake and the Upper Hoh River (Martin Creek, Elk Lake, Glacier Meadows); itinerary changes must be made on Recreation.gov or at a WIC before the trip; camp only in the camp area on your permit for that night.

Maximum group size 12 people and 8 stock. On the Hoh River Trail and Hoh Lake Trail, individual sites are limited to 6; groups of 7-12 must use designated group sites. Affiliated groups may not combine above 12 and must camp and travel at least 1 mile apart.

All food, garbage and scented items must be stored in park-approved animal-resistant food containers (bear canisters) for overnight stays anywhere in the wilderness; bear wires and self-built hangs are not appropriate; Ursack is not on the approved list. Canisters can be borrowed free at the Port Angeles WIC and Quinault station.

Campfires prohibited above 3,500 ft park-wide. On the Hoh: no campfires at or above Elk Lake (NPS 2026 conditions; trail page says none above Martin Creek); none at Hoh Lake or C.B. Flats. Where allowed, use dead and down wood in existing rings or on gravel bars and leave no trace.
No camping between Glacier Meadows and the Blue Glacier; climbers camp at Caltech Rocks and Snow Dome.
WAG/blue bags are required on Mount Olympus; there is no blue-bag deposit on the lateral moraine - pack it out (bags at the Hoh VC or Port Angeles WIC).
Mount Olympus should only be attempted by experienced mountaineers with glacier travel and crevasse rescue skills and gear; NPS best season late June through mid-August.

Stock may not camp above Martin Creek; in 2026 stock are closed beyond Martin Creek except llamas; Hoh Lake Trail is day-use only for stock and not currently stock passable; nature trails closed to stock.
Pets, bicycles and other wheeled devices are prohibited on park trails; drones prohibited; use of firearms prohibited.

Use toilets where provided (Hoh: Five Mile Island, Olympus Guard Station, Lewis Meadow, Elk Lake, Glacier Meadows; C.B. Flats/Hoh Lake). Elsewhere bury waste 6-8 inches deep at least 200 ft from water, camps and trails, and pack out toilet paper.
Treat all water (boil, filter or chemical) to prevent Giardia.
No fishing license is required inside the park; park fishing regulations apply.
Stay at least 50 yards from wildlife (2015 park release); the park's elk page asks for at least 100 feet from elk. Approaching or feeding wildlife is illegal.
A park entrance pass is required at the Hoh entrance station (interagency annual passes accepted).
A Washington Discover Pass is required at the South Fork Hoh trailhead (state DNR land).
Camp only in designated sites on durable bare ground; on the Hoh, river gravel bars are encouraged as low-impact sites.

conditions_2026.note: NPS alerts: Hoh Rain Forest area, trails, parking and restrooms open; visitor center open daily 9 am-4:30 pm; summer entrance waits up to 2 hours (arrive before 8 am or after 5 pm). Hoh Campground open; reservations were required June 12-September 6, 2026. Queets roads and primitive campground open, subject to short-notice weather closures.

Upper Hoh Road open, 18 mi paved from Hwy 101 (NPS road page, last road update 5/5/26). An earlier 2026 version of the page warned of one-way traffic and up to 20-minute delays late May-August for storm repairs at mileposts 0.3 and 0.8.

The December 10, 2025 atmospheric-river storm flooded Upper Hoh Road near milepost 10, cutting off the Hoh Rain Forest for about a month; reopening was expected the first week of January 2026. (Separately, a December 2024 washout at MP 9.7 closed the road until May 8, 2025.) The road is chronically vulnerable to Hoh River floods.

US 101 Hoh River Bridge (MP 176.5) emergency repair: one-lane alternating signals and 25 mph since July 14, 2026; nightly closures Sept 15-22; full closures 5 am Sept 24-5 pm Sept 29, 5 am Oct 1-noon Oct 6, and 5 am Oct 8-noon Oct 13, 2026; no detour across the Hoh (about 4 hours around Hood Canal). Single lane until a long-term repair; project runs to Sept 2028.

Hoh River Trail (trailhead to Glacier Meadows, 17.5 mi): two stream crossings before Olympus Guard Station must be forded (low 06/01/26; can become impassable in moderate/heavy rain); 37 downed trees between trailhead and Glacier Meadows; stock passable to OGS (05/29/26); stock hitching post at 5 Mile Island washed away; stock closed beyond Martin Creek except llamas; avalanche-chute ladder has 3 broken rungs and 1 missing; no campfires at or above Elk Lake; Martin Creek, Elk Lake and Glacier Meadows are quota areas.

Trip report (June 14-17, 2026): the ladder is anchored to a dead tree with over 50% of its roots exposed; two rungs broken and at least five cracked; real rockfall risk, helmets recommended; writer would not be surprised if it collapsed this year. Another report (June 19-22, 2026) found a midday queue at the ladder.

Trip report (May 2026): two crossings between Happy Four and Olympus Guard Station mostly dry or very shallow; privies at Five Mile Island and OGS in good order; told bear bags no longer allowed in 2026.

Winter damage reported January 2026: large blowdown ~0.25 mi past Mount Tom Creek; two washouts before Mineral Creek (one needing a steep loose-rock detour); a 50-ft flooded section ~1 mi before Five Mile Island; a creek cutting the embankment ~1 mi past Happy Four. Likely addressed or changed since; treat as possibly stale.
Hoh Lake Trail (Hoh River Trail to High Divide jct., 6.5 mi): cleared of downed trees and brushed; steep, exposed grade through the 1978 burn; no water until C.B. Flats; not stock passable.

Mount Olympus: no recent NPS reports as of 06/14/26; WAG bags required, no blue-bag deposit on the lateral moraine. June 2026 climber reports: moraine descent still very poor; the direct Fourth of July route was in good shape in June 2026 (in 2025 its last bergschrund snow bridge collapsed, forcing Crystal Pass).
South Fork Hoh River Trail (trailhead to end of maintained trail, 4.2 mi): no recent report.

Bogachiel River Trail (boundary to Mink Lake & Little Divide jct., 21.6 mi): washed out just before Mosquito Creek (steep detour with a short exposed section); washed out between Flapjack and 15 Mile (difficult to navigate around); most established sites at Bogachiel Camp eroded into the river - camp on the river bar at low water; creek and river crossings can become hazardous at any time.

North Snider-Jackson (boundary to Bogachiel jct., 6.3 mi): no trailhead signage; Calawah ford can become hazardous; not recommended for stock. South Snider-Jackson (South Bank Trail jct. to Hoh Road, 10.0 mi): Bogachiel must be forded and often runs deep; not stock passable; Tumwata Creek at the north end is the only water.
Rugged Ridge (North Snider-Jackson) trailhead road closed near the FS 29 (Sitkum Sol Duc Road) junction due to road failure, expected through September 2026.

Queets River Trail (trailhead to Pelton Creek, 16.2 mi): 18 downed trees between the ford and Spruce Bottom and 11 between Spruce Bottom and Bob Creek; brushy, thorny fields make the trail hard to find; the ford is dangerous (more likely fordable below 800 cfs at Hwy 101; can still be waist deep or deeper; generally not fordable late fall to spring; can rise within hours); ~200-yard washout 0.3 mi west of Bob Creek with a riverside bypass; past Bob Creek hard to follow after the 2015 Paradise Fire and camping not recommended (standing dead trees). Lower Crossing Route, Sam's River Loop and Upper Crossing Route: no recent reports (6/15/26).

Food storage: approved animal-resistant food containers required in all wilderness areas; approved list updated 6/25/2026; page updated 7/7/2026. Recreation.gov states bear wires and hangs are prohibited / not appropriate in 2026, even where older NPS camp data lists bear wires (Mount Tom Creek, Happy Four, OGS, Lewis Meadow, Elk Lake, Glacier Meadows, C.B. Flats, Hoh Lake).
Glacier Meadows camp (2025 reports): creek low by September (6-8 inch pools); some tent sites under dead trees; group-site pads flooded in a downpour.
Upper Bogachiel (2025 reports): Hyak-15 Mile stretch heavily overgrown and wet; 21 Mile shelter gone (pile of wood), campsite in good shape; trail crew working west of Flapjack.

High Hoh Bridge mileage: Oregon Hikers says 13.1; GIS geometry and camp ordering put it between the 13.1 and 13.2 sites (13.15 used). Its elevation (~1,340 ft) is a DEM value at the gorge crossing, not a surveyed deck height.

Node elevations without a published figure were sampled from the USGS 3DEP 10 m DEM (EPQS/OpenTopoData) at NPS/OSM coordinates or along NPS trail geometry; segment gain/loss values are DEM-derived with a 15 ft noise filter and are approximate.
Glacier Meadows elevation 4,300 ft is the NPS figure; the DEM at the NPS camp coordinate reads ~4,175-4,190 ft.

Glacier Meadows ladder: exact position (~1/4 mile before camp per Recreation.gov/NPS) and height (~100 ft per guide descriptions) are approximate; condition changes yearly and the ladder may fail or be replaced.

Mount Olympus climb segments (moraine descent, glacier crossing, Caltech Rocks, Snow Dome, Crystal Pass, false summit, summit block) have no official mileages; the 0.2/0.9/0.5/0.8/0.6/0.3-mile values are estimates scaled to NPS's 4-6 mi Glacier Meadows-to-summit and a guide's ~1 mile of glacier.

Caltech Rocks and the false summit have no verified elevation or coordinates. Snow Dome elevation 6,786 ft is the DEM at the OSM-mapped point; reports give camp at 6,600-6,800 ft and guides say 7,000 ft. Crystal Pass 7,250 ft (NWAG) vs 7,200 ft (Madison Mountaineering).
Blue Glacier surface elevation at the climbers' descent (~4,700 ft) is derived from the 5,100-ft moraine crest minus a reported ~400 ft scree descent.
Terminal moraine viewpoint (elevation ~4,200 ft, 0.4 mi from the junction) comes only from the anecdotal Oregon Hikers guide; coordinates unknown.
Hoh Lake Trail: C.B. Flats at 4.5 mi from the junction derived from NPS (Hoh Lake 14.7 mi from trailhead; C.B. Flats 0.5 mi south of the lake). WTA lists 4.7 mi to Hoh Lake.
